pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: Clear urine turning dark port-wine color upon light exposure, accompanied by neurovisceral pain, SIADH-induced hyponatremia, and catastrophic neurological collapse following the administration of a potent CYP450 inducer (phenytoin) in the setting of severe caloric restriction. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant inborn error of heme biosynthesis caused by a deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD, also known as hydroxymethylbilane synthase). Starvation depresses hepatic glycogen reserves, leading to the disinhibition and induction of ALAS1 (aminolevulinic acid synthase 1). The administration of CYP450-inducing xenobiotics like phenytoin further aggressively drives ALAS1 activity. Because of the enzymatic bottleneck at PBGD, non-toxic pathway progression is blocked, causing an immense, catastrophic accumulation of upstream neurotoxic heme precursors: delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). ALA and PBG cause direct autonomic toxicity (hypertension, tachycardia), central neurotoxicity (hallucinations, seizures, hypothalamic SIADH-driven hyponatremia), and severe motor axonal neuropathy (ascending quadriparesis and respiratory failure). Treatment demands immediate withdrawal of porphyrogenic drugs, aggressive intravenous dextrose administration to suppress ALAS1 transcription, and urgent intravenous hemin to restore heme pools and shut down the biochemical cascade.
